On the positive side, the survey of projects relocatees indicates that many have medium incomes. These may purchase new homes on the private sales market and will not draw heavily on the available public or subsidized units.
There are major positive factors which serve to offset some of these negative aspects of displacement. First, the Real Property Acquisition and Relocation Act of 1970 requires displacing agencies (using federal funds) to provide:
(a)Relocation assistance and counseling, and
(b)more generous relocation payments than had previously
been authorized. Therefore, while displacement is traumatic, it
can be alleviated by assistance and counseling. The Harrisburg
Redevelopment Agency has agreed to comply with this requirement.
The relocation payments required by the law (described in Part I)
serve to reduce, if not eliminate, the financial burdens most
relocatees experience. Indeed, provisions of the law allow
some relocatees to improve their economic situation either
by allowing homeowners to buy new homes without mortgages or
tenants to move into the more advantageous homeownership status.
Again, the Harrisburg Redevelopment Agency has agreed to comply
with these provisions.
Finally, and perhaps most importantly, the law also requires that the housing to which families and individuals are relocated be decent, safe, and sanitary. In most cases, this requirement results in families and individuals improving their housing situation. As mentioned above, many of the flood victims are anticipating this aid as a relief measure to offset the loss experienced as a result of the 1972 flood.
On balance, however, it appears that the adverse effects of relocation are outweighed by the benefits, especially in the unique situations involving flood disaster relief.
Loss to the tax base of the local taxing jurisdictions cannot be avoided in the short-run due to the public acquisition of project property and its remaining in the public domain for a length of time. As discussed previously this loss will eventually be offset by the appreciation of properties within the project, and general area of the project, as a result of the positive influences introduced by project activity. The actual loss may not be as great as it appears since a large portion of the properties to be acquired were damaged by flooding. The County Tax Assessor, under special state legislation, has subsequently reduced the assessment value of many of these flood damaged properties. Only 9 of the properties to be acquired are in a standard condition.
